set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 42) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate while answering some of the questions.
According to the Central Pollution Control Board, India generated over 3.47 million tonnes of plastic waste in 2019–20, and continues to rise unchecked. A 2021 study conducted by Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi had detected microplastics not only in rivers and lakes, but also in treated drinking water in major cities like Delhi and Mumbai. This reveals that even water deemed safe for households and consumption isn’t entirely plastic-free. Globally, the World Wildlife Fund’s No Plastic in Nature report has estimated that the average person could be ingesting up to 5 grams of microplastics per week—roughly the size of a credit card. Yes, that means you may have eaten plastic last night! This is not just because of faraway ocean waste, but very likely due to the garbage piling up in your own neighbourhood. Studies into Indian urban cities revealed the ugly truth—microplastics present in overflowing landfills and sewage _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_ plastic. Over time, this **mismanaged** waste breaks down into microplastics that seep into the soil, water, and air, and eventually, into our food. This **alarming** crisis is not just about plastic. It is about responsibility. Until our mindset towards waste accountability changes, laws will fail. Although there is a strict need for stringent laws and policies, we also need a solution that motivates action in individuals, not through punishment, but by rewarding it. A system that makes responsibility feels worth it.
This is where the ‘Plastic Reward System’ steps in. It turns waste management into a value-driven process for both citizens and industries. The Plastic Reward System encourages industries and communities to treat plastic as a resource instead. At the industrial level, companies that recycle plastic into useful products like 3D printer filaments or convert it into fuel through pyrolysis receive tax credits. Those who exceed their targets can even sell extra credits to other companies, creating a plastic credit market. This transforms waste management into a viable, profitable model. At the community level, schools, resident groups, and local cooperatives can set up plastic collection points and track the gathered amount of waste. Their efforts earn plastic credits, redeemable as cash incentives, school supplies, or community benefits. Whether it’s recycled bricks, tiles, or bags, innovation at the ground level is encouraged and celebrated. This system transforms plastic from a nuisance into a shared mission. It builds a culture where doing the right thing isn’t just expected, it’s rewarded. Plastic is just the symptom. Responsibility is the cure—and that starts with all of us.
stem: Why does the passage suggest a reward system is more effective than strict laws alone?

options.a: Laws are completely unnecessary for waste management.
options.b: Rewards create a mindset shift and encourage voluntary responsibility.
options.c: Punishments are more motivating than rewards.
options.d: Communities cannot participate in waste management.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 41) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
People living in Delhi are losing over eight years of their lives due to toxic air. This means that if the air quality in the national capital was improved to meet the standards of the World Health Organization (WHO), an average Delhi resident could live 8.2 years longer, new research by The Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) has found. The loss in life expectancy to high PM2.5 (particulate matter 2.5) was globally the highest in National Capital Territory (NCT) Delhi, according to the report titled, Air Quality Life Index (AQLI), that analysed air quality data of the year 2023. Meanwhile, on average, an Indian resident could live 3.5 years longer if pollution levels were brought down. Globally, if particulate pollution were permanently reduced to meet this guideline, an average person around the world would gain 1.9 years of life, adding 15.1 billion total life years to the global population.
In India, an average resident of the Indo-Gangetic Plains of North India could live five years longer if particulate concentrations met the WHO guideline of 5 microgram per cubic metre (µg/m³). The Northern Plains are India’s most polluted region. Beyond the Northern Plains, the states of Chhattisgarh, Tripura and Jharkhand were the most polluted in the country, the research revealed. On average, people living in these states could live 3.7 years longer. The findings are **crucial** from a public health perspective, especially at a time when the Indian government has not recognised any direct link between air pollution and mortality. While particulate pollution remained the greater external threat to human life expectancy, Union Minister of State for Health Anupriya Patel had told Parliament in July last year that there was no “conclusive data available in the country to establish a direct **correlation** of death/disease exclusively due to air pollution.”
The AQLI report released on August 28 said particulate pollution remained the greatest external threat to human life expectancy in 2023, with its impact comparable to smoking and surpassing other major health risks. Its **toll** on life expectancy is more than four times that of alcohol use, five times that of transport injuries or unsafe water, sanitation, and handwashing, and more than six times that of HIV/AIDS. In India, the country with the highest health burden of pollution in South Asia, the particulate concentration in 2023 was 41 µg/m³—more than eight times the WHO guideline, and slightly higher than the country’s national ambient PM2.5 standard of 40 µg/m³.
In response to the air quality crisis, the government had launched the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) in 2019. The research found that this has led to an increase of six months in life expectancy for 445.5 million people living in districts with ‘non-attainment cities’, where pollution levels have already declined by 10.7 per cent compared to 2017 levels.
stem: If Delhi were to reduce PM2.5 levels to meet WHO standards, what broader implication for public health does the passage suggest?

options.a: Residents would require more healthcare facilities.
options.e: Smoking rates would rise due to cleaner air.

passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Outer space was once imagined as an almost empty, serene theater in which a small handful of state agencies operated large, highly specialized satellites. That original image is now entirely obsolete. Today, tens of thousands of active commercial and military satellites share increasingly crowded orbital lanes with spent rocket upper stages, defunct spacecraft, and hundreds of thousands of hazardous fragments generated by accidental mid-air collisions and intentional anti-satellite missile tests. At orbital velocity—roughly seven to eight kilometers per second—even a paint-chip-sized piece of debris carries enough kinetic force to puncture critical equipment that would easily survive far larger impacts on Earth. Consequently, the orbital environment has become **congested** in a way that remains invisible from the ground, yet grows increasingly consequential for daily telecommunications, accurate weather forecasting, satellite navigation, global banking transactions, and emergency disaster relief operations.
The governance problem in low-Earth orbit is uniquely complex and demanding. Because no single sovereign nation owns space, it functions as an essential global commons, yet the heavy costs of operational negligence are shared indiscriminately by every user. A commercial enterprise or state actor that launches satellites cheaply reaps immediate economic benefits, while the heightened risk of a catastrophic collision is dispersed across rival operators, satellite insurers, and the billions of everyday citizens who rely on space-based services. Advanced ground-based tracking systems can monitor relatively large objects, but millions of smaller, high-velocity fragments remain completely untraceable. Furthermore, even when a modern satellite is explicitly engineered to de-orbit at the end of its mission, a malfunctioning battery, depleted fuel reserve, or sudden communications failure can instantly transform good operational intentions into permanent space debris.
In response, international space policy has gradually begun to focus on practical hazard _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_: designing spacecraft capable of automated end-of-life maneuvers, passivating residual fuel tanks to prevent spontaneous explosions, and requiring operators to share real-time positional data. However, reliance on voluntary guidelines is no longer sufficient in an increasingly saturated orbital ecosystem. Enforceable licensing rules, mandatory third-party insurance requirements, and strict **liability** standards must be established globally so that debris prevention becomes an unavoidable, standard cost of doing business rather than an optional corporate virtue.
The issue strongly resembles terrestrial environmental degradation, except that the pollution in question travels at hyper-velocity speeds. If regulators wait to enforce binding international standards until after a chain-reaction cascade of collisions renders key orbits unusable, the global space economy will suffer severe, lasting harm. Ultimately, building a sustainable economic future in space will depend far less on the spectacle of rocket launches than on the **unglamorous**, disciplined responsibility of managing and cleaning up after them.
stem:
As discussed in the passage, which of the following factors actively contribute to orbital collision risk?
A) Spent rocket upper stages and inactive spacecraft remain in shared orbital lanes.
B) Hazardous fragments are created by accidental mid-air collisions and test debris.
C) Millions of smaller, high-velocity fragments remain completely untraceable.
D) Space debris travels at speeds far too low to cause physical equipment damage.

options.e: All A, B, C, and D

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Outer space was once imagined as an almost empty, serene theater in which a small handful of state agencies operated large, highly specialized satellites. That original image is now entirely obsolete. Today, tens of thousands of active commercial and military satellites share increasingly crowded orbital lanes with spent rocket upper stages, defunct spacecraft, and hundreds of thousands of hazardous fragments generated by accidental mid-air collisions and intentional anti-satellite missile tests. At orbital velocity—roughly seven to eight kilometers per second—even a paint-chip-sized piece of debris carries enough kinetic force to puncture critical equipment that would easily survive far larger impacts on Earth. Consequently, the orbital environment has become **congested** in a way that remains invisible from the ground, yet grows increasingly consequential for daily telecommunications, accurate weather forecasting, satellite navigation, global banking transactions, and emergency disaster relief operations.
The governance problem in low-Earth orbit is uniquely complex and demanding. Because no single sovereign nation owns space, it functions as an essential global commons, yet the heavy costs of operational negligence are shared indiscriminately by every user. A commercial enterprise or state actor that launches satellites cheaply reaps immediate economic benefits, while the heightened risk of a catastrophic collision is dispersed across rival operators, satellite insurers, and the billions of everyday citizens who rely on space-based services. Advanced ground-based tracking systems can monitor relatively large objects, but millions of smaller, high-velocity fragments remain completely untraceable. Furthermore, even when a modern satellite is explicitly engineered to de-orbit at the end of its mission, a malfunctioning battery, depleted fuel reserve, or sudden communications failure can instantly transform good operational intentions into permanent space debris.
In response, international space policy has gradually begun to focus on practical hazard _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_: designing spacecraft capable of automated end-of-life maneuvers, passivating residual fuel tanks to prevent spontaneous explosions, and requiring operators to share real-time positional data. However, reliance on voluntary guidelines is no longer sufficient in an increasingly saturated orbital ecosystem. Enforceable licensing rules, mandatory third-party insurance requirements, and strict **liability** standards must be established globally so that debris prevention becomes an unavoidable, standard cost of doing business rather than an optional corporate virtue.
The issue strongly resembles terrestrial environmental degradation, except that the pollution in question travels at hyper-velocity speeds. If regulators wait to enforce binding international standards until after a chain-reaction cascade of collisions renders key orbits unusable, the global space economy will suffer severe, lasting harm. Ultimately, building a sustainable economic future in space will depend far less on the spectacle of rocket launches than on the **unglamorous**, disciplined responsibility of managing and cleaning up after them.
stem: As explicitly stated in the passage, the governance problem in low-Earth orbit is unusual because _​_​_​_​_​_​_

options.a: low-Earth orbit is owned by a single private corporation that dictates standard operational policy.
options.b: recent reductions in launch expenditures have rendered debris prevention entirely cost-prohibitive.
options.c: essential space services are completely disconnected from terrestrial banking and disaster operations.
options.d: small orbital fragments can easily be collected and neutralized using atmospheric weather balloons.
options.e: no single nation holds ownership over orbit, yet operational negligence imposes shared global costs.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 39) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are **highlighted** to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Cartographers, urban planners and geospatial analysts spend their working days in sustained spatial reasoning. A geographic information system specialist might use a computer to overlap population data on flood exposure maps to find who is at risk, or read satellite imagery to map land cover after a wildfire. Researchers **juggle** several layers of data, coordinate systems and scales at once.
Does spatial reasoning through a screen engage the hippocampus the way moving through a real city does?
While a taxi driver navigates from inside the scene at street level, GIS researchers picture space from above as a map – what cognitive scientists call allocentric reasoning. But these two perspectives overlap in the brain: The hippocampus also builds maps from outside viewpoints, not just from a navigator’s own position.
Research on cognitive maps points toward the same conclusion as the study on taxi drivers. In 2023, researchers ran a machine learning model on more than 22,500 people in a national dataset and were able to predict which ZIP codes had higher rates of Alzheimer’s with 84% accuracy based on how **complex** the environment was. Those living in spatially complex surroundings – the kind that force active map building, such as dense street networks with numerous intersections, diverse points of interest and landmarks, and multiple path options – were less likely to develop Alzheimer’s. A follow-up study tied geospatial complexity in one’s environment to greater volume in the brain’s spatial navigation regions. The researchers **hypothesized** that routinely building cognitive maps exercises the very circuitry that Alzheimer’s attacks first. Repeatedly engaging the cognitive systems involved in spatial navigation could help delay symptoms of disease.
However, these two studies focus on where people live, not the work people do. Whether spatial reasoning through a screen exercises the same circuitry as real-life city navigation remains untested.
The implications of whether sustained spatial reasoning protects the brain reach beyond mapmakers and cab drivers. Studies have repeatedly found a link between mentally _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_ occupations and delayed cognitive decline and lower dementia risk, even after accounting for education.
Research on cognitive reserve – the brain’s capacity to continue functioning despite disease – can help explain why two people with a similar disease burden can show markedly different levels of cognitive impairment. If demanding spatial thinking protects the brain, then how societies design schooling, professional training and retirement all become questions of brain health.
Spatial reasoning can be trained, and training opportunities are already widespread. GIS and remote sensing instruction are available through geography, engineering, public health and environmental science programs worldwide.
If sustained engagement with spatial reasoning can help the brain strengthen the circuitry that Alzheimer’s attacks first, its value reaches well beyond the technical skills it builds.

options.a: To analyze how spatial thinking can protect human brain health.
options.b: To prove that taxi drivers possess superior cognitive capacity.
options.c: To explain how modern digital software operates in research.
options.d: To argue that urban residence prevents all cognitive decline.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 38) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given. Certain words/phrases have been given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Indian cities often announce ambitious infrastructure plans, but the financing behind them remains fragile. Property taxes are politically unpopular, user charges rarely cover maintenance, and grants from higher levels of government can arrive late or be tied to centrally chosen priorities. Municipal bonds appear to offer a way out: a city can borrow today for a drainage network, bus depot or water-treatment plant and repay investors over time from predictable revenue streams. The instrument, however, is not a magical substitute for fiscal discipline.
Investors do not buy a city’s promise; they buy its ability to keep that promise. A municipality that wants to issue bonds must publish audited accounts, disclose existing liabilities and identify the revenue that will service the debt. Some bond structures also require an escrow account into which taxes or user charges are paid before other expenses are met. This arrangement can **shore up** investor confidence because repayment is not left to annual political bargaining. In a few cases, state guarantees or pooled finance mechanisms have helped smaller towns approach the market together, reducing the risk that any single local body’s weakness will make the entire issue unattractive.
Yet the appeal of bonds can become dangerous if elected councils treat borrowing as prestige. A road that produces no additional revenue may still be worth building, but its repayment must come from somewhere. If optimistic traffic forecasts, inflated land values or delayed tariff revisions are used to justify debt, the bond merely pushes today’s discomfort into tomorrow’s budget. Transparency also matters. Bond documents often contain **covenants** about reporting, reserve funds and the permitted use of money. When these are written in dense language or monitored casually, citizens may discover the obligations only after services are cut to meet repayment schedules.
The better argument for municipal bonds is therefore conditional. They can finance durable assets, create pressure for better accounts and attract long-term capital into urban infrastructure. But they work best when citizens can see what is being borrowed, why it is being borrowed, and how it will be repaid. If the discipline of the bond market is matched by the discipline of democratic disclosure, borrowing can become a tool of civic capacity rather than a device for postponing hard choices.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 37) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Machine translation is often advertised as a universal **solvent** for linguistic barriers. For widely used languages with vast digital corpora, the claim can seem plausible. A tourist can point a phone at a menu, a researcher can skim a foreign abstract, and an official notice can be roughly understood across borders. But the technology becomes less miraculous when the language in question has little written data, multiple dialects, or a writing system that has only recently been standardised. Low-resource languages expose the limits of models that learn largely from what the internet has already made abundant. Their difficulties reveal that technological progress in translation is not evenly distributed across the world’s linguistic landscape.
The difficulty is not merely technical. A language may have rich oral traditions but few digitised texts. Elders may possess vocabulary that younger speakers no longer use, while community members may disagree about spelling, script, or the terms that should be used for modern institutions. In some communities, the same word may carry different meanings depending on the speaker, region, occasion, or social relationship. If engineers collect speech without consent, or translate sacred narratives into open datasets, a tool meant to protect language can become another form of extraction. Communities therefore increasingly ask not only whether a translation system works, but who controls the data, who decides acceptable usage, and who benefits from commercial deployment.
There are promising alternatives. Some projects train smaller models in partnership with speakers, allowing communities to restrict sensitive material while still building dictionaries, educational tools, and public-service translation. Others use translation technology as a support for human interpreters rather than a replacement for them. This matters because meaning is often **situated.** A word used in a legal notice, a folk tale, and a condolence message may require different choices even when a dictionary gives the same English equivalent. Fluency that ignores social context can be dangerously misleading, particularly when translations influence education, healthcare, legal rights, or communication between public institutions and citizens.
The future of translation for low-resource languages will depend on a shift in imagination. The goal should not be to absorb every language into a single automated marketplace, but to give speakers more control over how their language travels. Technology should be designed with communities rather than merely for them, and local knowledge should be treated as more than raw material for training algorithms. If technology strengthens consent, documentation, education, and intergenerational learning, it can help fragile languages endure. If it treats them only as data, it may accelerate the very loss it claims to prevent.
stem: According to the first paragraph, what primary factor exposes the current limitations of machine translation models?

options.a: The lack of universal interest among international research teams.
options.b: The lack of interest from local communities in preserving traditions.
options.c: The lack of standardized hardware systems used for mobile translation.
options.d: The lack of abundant digital data available for low-resource languages.
options.e: The lack of financial support provided by global public institutions.

Elders may possess vocabulary that younger speakers no longer use, while community members may disagree about spelling, script, or the terms that should be used for modern institutions. In some communities, the same word may carry different meanings depending on the speaker, region, occasion, or social relationship. If engineers collect speech without consent, or translate sacred narratives into open datasets, a tool meant to protect language can become another form of extraction. Communities therefore increasingly ask not only whether a translation system works, but who controls the data, who decides acceptable usage, and who benefits from commercial deployment.
There are promising alternatives. Some projects train smaller models in partnership with speakers, allowing communities to restrict sensitive material while still building dictionaries, educational tools, and public-service translation. Others use translation technology as a support for human interpreters rather than a replacement for them. This matters because meaning is often **situated.** A word used in a legal notice, a folk tale, and a condolence message may require different choices even when a dictionary gives the same English equivalent. Fluency that ignores social context can be dangerously misleading, particularly when translations influence education, healthcare, legal rights, or communication between public institutions and citizens.
The future of translation for low-resource languages will depend on a shift in imagination. The goal should not be to absorb every language into a single automated marketplace, but to give speakers more control over how their language travels. Technology should be designed with communities rather than merely for them, and local knowledge should be treated as more than raw material for training algorithms. If technology strengthens consent, documentation, education, and intergenerational learning, it can help fragile languages endure. If it treats them only as data, it may accelerate the very loss it claims to prevent.

India’s rise on the global stage is reshaping economic and diplomatic priorities across the Indo-Pacific region. As its economy expands and its young population enters the workforce, the country is increasingly becoming an important partner for nations seeking stronger regional cooperation. India is the world’s most populous democracy and will, by 2030, be the most populous country, overtaking China. And it is young — there are more Indian 10-year-olds than there are Australians. With more than a dozen distinct languages, scripts and religions, India is multiculturalism on the grandest scale. And to sustain a **vibrant** modern democracy, surely India is one of the greatest political achievements of our times. Once you appreciate its size, you see its potential. Think of all those 10-year-olds who will one day be voting in India’s elections and who will also, one day, belong to India’s middle class, the engine of its **booming** economy. Put all that together and it’s easy to **understand (B)** why India will play a central role in our **relationship (C)** and the world and, I hope for Australians, it is easier to see why the **region (D)** between our two countries has never been more important. That formal relationship began for many Australians in 1950, when Robert Menzies became the first Australian leader to visit independent India. Since then, both countries have been transformed. Now we must turn our attention to transforming the relationship to one that matches India’s huge needs and its enormous potential with our people, Australia’s best assets, as well as our resources and our shared democratic traditions. India is inspiring the world with its explosive economic growth. Its economic **(A) _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_** is lifting millions out of poverty, transforming the country into the world’s fastest-growing major economy, with forecasted growth of 7.5% in 2017. This is a stunning result for India, and a rare opportunity for Australia. From Mumbai to Melbourne, from Bengaluru to Brisbane, India will be in the market to buy some of the best things Australia has to offer. Two-way trade is growing, and approaching $20 billion, but that’s far too low and there’s so much more we can do. This will be a key focus of my visit. I’ll meet with executives from some of India’s biggest companies, and speak with Australian entrepreneurs in India who are expanding their market reach into this extraordinary country.

passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
The modern gig economy, initially **heralded** as a utopia of freelance flexibility and entrepreneurial freedom, has rapidly morphed into a complex ecosystem governed by algorithmic management. Platforms offering ride-hailing, food delivery, and micro-tasks rely on proprietary algorithms to allocate work, determine dynamic pricing, and monitor worker performance in real-time. For consumers, this translates to seamless, on-demand convenience and a service model that operates with remarkable speed and efficiency. However, for the independent contractors powering these platforms, the reality is often characterized by extreme income volatility, uncertain working hours, and a profound lack of autonomy.
At the heart of this tension is the concept of information asymmetry. Gig workers operate under **opaque** algorithmic directives where the rules of engagement can change overnight without meaningful human mediation. A worker may not fully understand why certain tasks are assigned, why earnings fluctuate, or how performance ratings influence future opportunities. Platforms frequently employ behavioral nudges and gamification techniques—such as arbitrary bonus streaks, achievement targets, and personalized push notifications—to keep workers logged in during high-demand periods. This relentless digital optimization treats human labor as a highly elastic commodity that can be expanded or contracted according to market demand. Consequently, workers are locked in a perpetual cycle of chasing fluctuating incentives, often bearing the brunt of hidden operational costs such as vehicle maintenance, fuel, mobile data, and health insurance, which traditional employers would otherwise cover.
The growing unrest among gig workers has catalyzed a global legal and regulatory **reckoning.** Labor advocates argue that algorithmic control is practically indistinguishable from traditional managerial oversight, thereby entitling gig workers to statutory benefits such as minimum wage guarantees, paid leave, workplace protections, and social security. Several jurisdictions have already passed landmark rulings reclassifying specific independent contractors as formal employees, while others are exploring hybrid categories that could provide protections without eliminating the flexibility associated with gig work. At the same time, platforms warn that excessive regulation could increase operational costs and reduce the availability of affordable, on-demand services.
Moving forward, the challenge for policymakers is not to dismantle the gig economy entirely, but to forge a new social contract that preserves technological efficiency **_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_(P)_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_** and greater accountability in algorithmic decision-making. The future of gig work will ultimately depend on whether innovation can be reconciled with the dignity and security of the people whose labor sustains it.

options.a: To provide workers with predictable earnings and guaranteed employment benefits.
options.b: To explain clearly how platforms determine prices and allocate available tasks.
options.c: To encourage workers to remain active during periods of high consumer demand.
options.d: To compensate workers for expenses related to fuel, insurance, and vehicle maintenance.
options.e: To help workers obtain formal employment status within the platform economy.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 34) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Let me tell you something we all know but rarely say out loud. Somewhere, right now, a hiring manager is sitting across from a candidate who looks great on paper. Confident. Well-spoken. Impressive CV. The interview goes well, the team likes them, and an offer letter goes out within the week. Nobody asks too many questions. Nobody digs too deep. There is a position to fill, and this person seems right. Three months later, something doesn’t add up. This is not a rare story. It happens more often than organisations care to admit, and the reason is almost always the same: background verification was skipped, rushed, or treated as a **formality** rather than a filter. We live in a country where getting a passport requires you to prove who you are, down to your grandmother’s address. A bank will not open an account without seeing your PAN, your Aadhaar, a photograph, a signature, and sometimes requiring a physical visit. A SIM card also requires documentation. The government, financial institutions, and even telecom providers have decided that verification is non-negotiable. They have built entire systems around it. And yet a company will hand someone a laptop, access to client data, a salary, and the trust of an entire team based on a CV they wrote themselves and two referees they personally selected. That logic seems strange when you lay it out plainly. The counter-arguments are understandable. Hiring is slow enough already. Good candidates do not wait. Documentation is sometimes genuinely incomplete. And honestly, when someone is sitting in front of you and they seem perfectly **decent**, asking for deeper verification can feel almost insulting. But that discomfort is exactly the point. The candidate who is perfectly decent has nothing to hide. They will wait the extra week. They will provide what is needed. The ones who push back hardest against verification are rarely the ones you want to be worried about, and yet somehow they are often the ones who slip through.
Incomplete documentation is not a reason to **skip** the process. It is a conversation to have before the offer, not a problem to quietly overlook. The cost of getting this wrong is not just financial, though that cost is real enough. It is the team that loses faith in leadership’s judgement. The client relationship that gets damaged. The culture that quietly shifts when someone with the wrong values sits inside it long enough. We do not let a stranger into our homes without knowing who they are. We should not let one into our organisations either. Background verification is not about distrust. It is about responsibility to the people already inside the organisation who deserve to work alongside someone who is exactly who they claim to be. Every hire is an act of faith. But faith, in the context of building teams, works best when it is backed by facts. Verify. Always.
stem: Replace the word “skip” with the most appropriate alternative.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 34) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Let me tell you something we all know but rarely say out loud. Somewhere, right now, a hiring manager is sitting across from a candidate who looks great on paper. Confident. Well-spoken. Impressive CV. The interview goes well, the team likes them, and an offer letter goes out within the week. Nobody asks too many questions. Nobody digs too deep. There is a position to fill, and this person seems right. Three months later, something doesn’t add up. This is not a rare story. It happens more often than organisations care to admit, and the reason is almost always the same: background verification was skipped, rushed, or treated as a **formality** rather than a filter. We live in a country where getting a passport requires you to prove who you are, down to your grandmother’s address. A bank will not open an account without seeing your PAN, your Aadhaar, a photograph, a signature, and sometimes requiring a physical visit. A SIM card also requires documentation. The government, financial institutions, and even telecom providers have decided that verification is non-negotiable. They have built entire systems around it. And yet a company will hand someone a laptop, access to client data, a salary, and the trust of an entire team based on a CV they wrote themselves and two referees they personally selected. That logic seems strange when you lay it out plainly. The counter-arguments are understandable. Hiring is slow enough already. Good candidates do not wait. Documentation is sometimes genuinely incomplete. And honestly, when someone is sitting in front of you and they seem perfectly **decent**, asking for deeper verification can feel almost insulting. But that discomfort is exactly the point. The candidate who is perfectly decent has nothing to hide. They will wait the extra week. They will provide what is needed. The ones who push back hardest against verification are rarely the ones you want to be worried about, and yet somehow they are often the ones who slip through.
Incomplete documentation is not a reason to **skip** the process. It is a conversation to have before the offer, not a problem to quietly overlook. The cost of getting this wrong is not just financial, though that cost is real enough. It is the team that loses faith in leadership’s judgement. The client relationship that gets damaged. The culture that quietly shifts when someone with the wrong values sits inside it long enough. We do not let a stranger into our homes without knowing who they are. We should not let one into our organisations either. Background verification is not about distrust. It is about responsibility to the people already inside the organisation who deserve to work alongside someone who is exactly who they claim to be. Every hire is an act of faith. But faith, in the context of building teams, works best when it is backed by facts. Verify. Always.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 33) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given. Certain words/phrases have been given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Over the past decade, Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria have transitioned from a niche ethical consideration into a dominant paradigm in global finance. Institutional investors, managing trillions of dollars in assets, are increasingly channeling capital toward corporations that ostensibly prioritize sustainability alongside profitability. This influx of capital has fueled the exponential growth of “green bonds” and sustainability-linked loans, allowing companies to finance eco-friendly projects at highly favorable interest rates. The **underlyingpremise** is compelling: free markets can, and should, be leveraged as powerful instruments for ecological preservation and social equity.
However, the rapid **proliferation** of ESG investing has outpaced the development of rigorous regulatory frameworks, creating a fertile environment for “greenwashing.” In the absence of a universally accepted taxonomy to define what is genuinely sustainable, companies frequently exploit **ambiguous** metrics to exaggerate or entirely fabricate their environmental credentials. For instance, a fossil fuel conglomerate might heavily publicize a minor investment in renewable energy while quietly expanding its core carbon-intensive operations. Such deceptive practices not only mislead well-intentioned investors but also introduce severe misallocation of capital. When funds meant to combat climate change are funneled into superficial public relations campaigns, the systemic integrity of the entire green finance market is jeopardized.
Recognizing the looming threat to market stability, financial watchdogs worldwide are pivoting from voluntary guidelines to mandatory disclosure regimes. Regulatory bodies are now demanding independently audited data regarding corporate carbon footprints, board diversity, and supply chain sustainability. This regulatory tightening aims to strip away the marketing veneer and hold corporations legally accountable for their environmental claims. Ultimately, for sustainable finance to fulfill its transformative potential, the market must transition to a state of absolute transparency, ensuring that capital is directed toward authentic climate solutions _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_.

options.a: To argue that all fossil fuel conglomerates should be immediately dismantled by financial regulators.
options.b: To analyze the rise of ESG investing, the systemic risks of greenwashing, and the subsequent regulatory crackdown.
options.c: To explain the mathematical formulas used to calculate interest rates on sustainability-linked loans.
options.d: To persuade everyday retail investors to stop investing in the stock market entirely.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 32) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
‘Gen Z’ has emerged as one of the most talked — about terms in India in recent past. The spotlight on this generation reflects a growing recognition that its aspirations, choices and capabilities will **profoundly** influence the country’s future. Yet an even bigger story is unfolding beyond the headlines. Gen Z is India’s first generation to step into higher education and the workplace in the age of AI. For the Baby Boomers, the defining technology was television. Generation X witnessed the rise of the personal computer. Millennials transformed the smartphone into an indispensable companion. Gen Z grew up in the age of social media, with platforms such as Instagram becoming integral to communication, creativity and self-expression. It is now the first generation to begin its professional journey alongside AI. Unlike earlier technological revolutions that unfolded over decades, AI is evolving at a remarkable speed. India is uniquely placed in this transformation. With one of the world’s youngest populations, the country possesses an extraordinary demographic advantage. Yet demographics alone do not guarantee prosperity. India’s demographic dividend will remain a statistic unless it is transformed into an economic and an AI dividend. That transformation will depend on whether its Gen Z are equipped to thrive in an AI-driven world.
India’s digital public infrastructure, expanding startup ecosystem and growing adoption of AI across sectors provide fertile ground for innovation. If educational institutions, industry and policymakers work in concert, the country has an opportunity not merely to participate in the global AI revolution, but to help shape it. AI is already changing the nature of work. Routine tasks such as drafting documents, analysing large volumes of data, scheduling activities and generating basic content are increasingly being automated. Consequently, employers are beginning to value qualities that machines cannot easily replicate, like critical thinking, creativity, ethical judgement, learning agility and emotional intelligence. AI is not simply changing jobs; it is changing the skills that make people employable. The future belongs to those **who can outthink AI.** This presents both an opportunity and a challenge for India’s Gen Z. Unlike earlier generations, today’s students have **unprecedented** access to powerful AI tools that can explain concepts, summarize information, generate ideas and accelerate learning. However, frequent use of AI should not be mistaken for AI literacy. Knowing how to use an AI application is very different from knowing how to frame effective prompts, verify responses, recognise inaccuracies and apply AI thoughtfully. True AI literacy also means understanding AI’s limitations, recognising bias, safeguarding privacy and knowing when human judgement must prevail. AI should become a thinking partner, not a thinking substitute.
stem: Which of the following best describes the central concern of the passage?

options.a: India’s inability to regulate the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence
options.b: India’s need to prepare Gen Z for an increasingly AI-driven future
options.c: India’s growing dependence on social media for professional communication
options.d: India’s failure to utilise its demographic advantage for economic development
options.e: India’s difficulty in balancing technological progress with educational reforms

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 31) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in bold to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Advertising is the strategic deployment of techniques and practices designed to bring products, services, opinions, or causes to public attention with the ultimate goal of persuading the audience to adopt a specific response. While the most common application is the promotion of goods for sale, often through sophisticated brand marketing, the principles of advertising extend to encouraging behaviors such as safe driving, supporting charitable causes, or influencing political choices. In many economies, advertising serves as a primary revenue stream for media outlets like newspapers, magazines, and television stations, solidifying its role as a significant service industry in the noncommunist world. The historical trajectory of advertising began with oral communication in ancient and medieval societies. The advent of the printing press in the 15th and 16th centuries laid the groundwork for modern advertising. By the 17th century, weekly newspapers in London were featuring advertisements, and this practice saw substantial growth throughout the 18th century. The 19th century witnessed a parallel expansion in business and the advertising industry, particularly in the United States, where the first advertising agencies were established. Initially acting as space brokers for newspapers, these agencies evolved by the early 20th century to encompass the creation of advertising content, including copy and artwork. By the 1920s, agencies were capable of managing comprehensive advertising campaigns, from initial market research to final media placement.
Advertising manifests across a wide spectrum of media. Newspapers offer broad reach and the ability to frequently update advertisements, while magazines cater to specific audiences, allowing manufacturers to target likely customers. Regional editions of national magazines further refine this targeting. In industrialized nations, radio and television have become dominant, with advertisers purchasing time slots for short commercials. The effectiveness of these spots is judged by audience size and composition. Other media include direct mail for personalized appeals, outdoor billboards and posters, and transit advertising reaching users of mass-transit systems. In the 21st century, digital technology has become increasingly vital for capturing consumer attention, with innovations like embedded video advertisements in print publications emerging. Ethical considerations are central to modern advertising practices. A significant concern involves the **surreptitious** online surveillance of consumers and the collection of their data without explicit consent or clear disclosure of usage, which can compromise consumer autonomy and protection from manipulation. Furthermore, advertisers are ethically bound to be mindful of cultural values and avoid offensive content, particularly when targeting vulnerable groups such as children. This includes ensuring messages are age-appropriate and promote positive values, rather than exploiting insecurities or promoting harmful products. The principle of social responsibility dictates that the interests of targeted individuals should be prioritized alongside those of for-profit companies.

options.a: To provide consumers with detailed product information
options.b: To persuade audiences to adopt a specific response
options.c: To generate financial support for various media outlets
options.d: To introduce innovative products into competitive markets
options.e: To encourage businesses to conduct extensive market research

passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in **bold** to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
From los angeles to London, weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic are reshaping culture as much as waistlines. Some Ozempic-takers have tiny appetites and dine at unusual hours to avoid spells of nausea. Others have lost their taste for alcohol. Many have given up on the gym, either because they are tired or because the drugs keep them svelte. My Ozempic Journey posts have racked up millions of views on TikTok, as people share how they are adjusting to their new lifestyles. These drugs have also slimmed people’s demand for diet books. Since June 2021, when Wegovy, the first blockbuster slimming jab, was approved by America’s Food and Drug Administration, sales of “health and fitness” print books in America have fallen by 15%, according to Circana, a research firm. (Sales of print books overall fell by 4%.) The category shifted fewer than 10m hard copies in the years ending June 2023 and June 2024, the lowest in a decade. Diet, exercise and weight-loss titles are among the worst sellers. Publishers are trying to fight back by _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_beyond books that promise fast results from calorie-counting and new dieting fads; they are focusing more on longevity and vitality. Living longer is the most exciting topic for readers today, says Olivia Morris, publishing director of Ebury Self, which released “Outlive” by Peter Attia, a doctor, in Britain last year. (It has sold more than 2m copies globally.) Sales of books about longevity rose by 50% in the past year, according to Circana. Another pocket of growth is women’s health. “The Cortisol Reset Plan”, to be published next year, investigates how the stress hormone causes female fatigue and weight gain.
Diet books that have achieved brisk sales, including Davinia Taylor’s “It’s Not A Diet” and Ben Carpenter’s “Everything Fat Loss”, tell readers to forget fads and make simple lifestyle changes. By promising low effort and high reward, they offer an easy, cheap alternative to drugs (which have a list price of more than $1,000 a month in America). There is also growing demand for “natural alternatives” to jabs, according to Victory Belt, a health publisher. On TikTok “nature’s Ozempic”—berberine, a plant extract claimed to promote weight loss— has gone viral. Publishers are not entirely **pessimistic** about injectable medicines. “Health and fitness” remains the ninth-largest adult non-fiction print book category in America. They are also faring better than others in the diet industry. The market value of ww (formerly Weight Watchers) has fallen by more than 90% since June 2021, with investors worried about growth prospects. In time the drugs may even lure new readers. Books are being written for those with suppressed appetites: “The Mayo Clinic Diet”, first published in 1949, has released a “weight-loss medications edition”. Some publishers predict greater demand for titles about diabetes and blood sugar, as people try to learn more about the science behind the drugs. (They mimic the hormones that the body produces after a meal to suppress appetite.) But as even cheaper and more convenient weight-loss drugs emerge and** spread**, publishers will probably need to change **tack.**

options.b: People dining at unusual hours to avoid nausea

From los angeles to London, weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic are reshaping culture as much as waistlines. Some Ozempic-takers have tiny appetites and dine at unusual hours to avoid spells of nausea. Others have lost their taste for alcohol. Many have given up on the gym, either because they are tired or because the drugs keep them svelte. My Ozempic Journey posts have racked up millions of views on TikTok, as people share how they are adjusting to their new lifestyles. These drugs have also slimmed people’s demand for diet books. Since June 2021, when Wegovy, the first blockbuster slimming jab, was approved by America’s Food and Drug Administration, sales of “health and fitness” print books in America have fallen by 15%, according to Circana, a research firm. (Sales of print books overall fell by 4%.) The category shifted fewer than 10m hard copies in the years ending June 2023 and June 2024, the lowest in a decade. Diet, exercise and weight-loss titles are among the worst sellers. Publishers are trying to fight back by _​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_​_beyond books that promise fast results from calorie-counting and new dieting fads; they are focusing more on longevity and vitality. Living longer is the most exciting topic for readers today, says Olivia Morris, publishing director of Ebury Self, which released “Outlive” by Peter Attia, a doctor, in Britain last year. (It has sold more than 2m copies globally.) Sales of books about longevity rose by 50% in the past year, according to Circana. Another pocket of growth is women’s health. “The Cortisol Reset Plan”, to be published next year, investigates how the stress hormone causes female fatigue and weight gain.
Diet books that have achieved brisk sales, including Davinia Taylor’s “It’s Not A Diet” and Ben Carpenter’s “Everything Fat Loss”, tell readers to forget fads and make simple lifestyle changes. By promising low effort and high reward, they offer an easy, cheap alternative to drugs (which have a list price of more than $1,000 a month in America). There is also growing demand for “natural alternatives” to jabs, according to Victory Belt, a health publisher. On TikTok “nature’s Ozempic”—berberine, a plant extract claimed to promote weight loss— has gone viral. Publishers are not entirely **pessimistic** about injectable medicines. “Health and fitness” remains the ninth-largest adult non-fiction print book category in America. They are also faring better than others in the diet industry. The market value of ww (formerly Weight Watchers) has fallen by more than 90% since June 2021, with investors worried about growth prospects. In time the drugs may even lure new readers. Books are being written for those with suppressed appetites: “The Mayo Clinic Diet”, first published in 1949, has released a “weight-loss medications edition”. Some publishers predict greater demand for titles about diabetes and blood sugar, as people try to learn more about the science behind the drugs. (They mimic the hormones that the body produces after a meal to suppress appetite.) But as even cheaper and more convenient weight-loss drugs emerge and** spread**, publishers will probably need to change **tack.**

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 29) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in **bold** to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
In a quiet corner of the academic world, a debate has simmered for decades regarding the precise nature of consciousness. Is it merely an emergent property of complex neural networks, reducible to the firing of synapses and the flow of electrochemical signals? Or does it possess a fundamentally different quality, perhaps a non-physical essence that transcends purely material explanations? This philosophical divide has significant implications, not only for neuroscience but also for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to ethics.
Proponents of the materialist view, often called physicalists, argue that consciousness is entirely a product of the brain. They point to advances in neuroimaging and brain lesion studies, which demonstrate a clear correlation between specific brain regions and conscious experiences. Damage to certain areas, for instance, can **obliterate** the ability to recognize faces, perceive color, or even form new memories. For physicalists, this evidence strongly suggests that consciousness arises directly from the brain’s physical architecture and activity. They often invoke the analogy of a complex computer program: the software (consciousness) is undeniably dependent on the hardware (brain).
Conversely, dualists and panpsychists contend that consciousness cannot be fully explained by physical processes alone. Dualists, dating back to Descartes, propose that mind and body are distinct substances. Modern dualists, while eschewing a strict Cartesian split, might argue for emergent properties that, once arisen, are no longer wholly explicable by their physical components. Panpsychists, on the other hand, take an even more radical stance, suggesting that consciousness, or proto-consciousness, is a fundamental feature of the universe, present in varying degrees even at the most basic levels of matter. They argue that if consciousness only appears at complex levels of organization, there is an explanatory **gap** regarding how it suddenly “switches on.”
The challenge for physicalists lies in explaining the subjective experience—the “what it is like” to be conscious—often referred to as qualia. While they can correlate brain states with experiences, they struggle to explain why those brain states produce that particular subjective feeling. For dualists, the challenge is the interaction problem: how does a non-physical mind interact with a physical brain? Panpsychists face the combination problem: how do tiny bits of consciousness combine to form complex conscious experiences?
As neuroscience continues to **unravel** the brain’s mysteries, the hope is that empirical evidence will eventually tip the scales. However, for now, the debate remains a fertile ground for philosophical inquiry, influencing how we design AI systems (should they ever truly be conscious?), understand mental illness, and even **frame** our understanding of free will and personal responsibility. The path to a definitive answer, if one exists, is still shrouded in the intricate workings of our own minds.

options.d: The historical philosophical divide between Descartes and modern thinkers.
options.e: The impact of brain lesions on perception.

Or does it possess a fundamentally different quality, perhaps a non-physical essence that transcends purely material explanations? This philosophical divide has significant implications, not only for neuroscience but also for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to ethics.
Proponents of the materialist view, often called physicalists, argue that consciousness is entirely a product of the brain. They point to advances in neuroimaging and brain lesion studies, which demonstrate a clear correlation between specific brain regions and conscious experiences. Damage to certain areas, for instance, can **obliterate** the ability to recognize faces, perceive color, or even form new memories. For physicalists, this evidence strongly suggests that consciousness arises directly from the brain’s physical architecture and activity. They often invoke the analogy of a complex computer program: the software (consciousness) is undeniably dependent on the hardware (brain).
Conversely, dualists and panpsychists contend that consciousness cannot be fully explained by physical processes alone. Dualists, dating back to Descartes, propose that mind and body are distinct substances. Modern dualists, while eschewing a strict Cartesian split, might argue for emergent properties that, once arisen, are no longer wholly explicable by their physical components. Panpsychists, on the other hand, take an even more radical stance, suggesting that consciousness, or proto-consciousness, is a fundamental feature of the universe, present in varying degrees even at the most basic levels of matter. They argue that if consciousness only appears at complex levels of organization, there is an explanatory **gap** regarding how it suddenly “switches on.”
The challenge for physicalists lies in explaining the subjective experience—the “what it is like” to be conscious—often referred to as qualia. While they can correlate brain states with experiences, they struggle to explain why those brain states produce that particular subjective feeling. For dualists, the challenge is the interaction problem: how does a non-physical mind interact with a physical brain? Panpsychists face the combination problem: how do tiny bits of consciousness combine to form complex conscious experiences?
As neuroscience continues to **unravel** the brain’s mysteries, the hope is that empirical evidence will eventually tip the scales. However, for now, the debate remains a fertile ground for philosophical inquiry, influencing how we design AI systems (should they ever truly be conscious?), understand mental illness, and even **frame** our understanding of free will and personal responsibility. The path to a definitive answer, if one exists, is still shrouded in the intricate workings of our own minds.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 28) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in **bold **to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
When he was the Indian government’s chief economist from 2014 to 2018, Arvind Subramanian made a surprising discovery. He drew an unexpectedly large audience for his annual “Economic Survey”, written on the eve of each year’s budget. As well as dry updates on tax revenues, inflation and grain production, his surveys included striking charts, provocative arguments and rhetorical flourishes. In 2016 he published a chart, bold in its simplicity, showing that democracy and development tended to go hand in hand. The big exceptions were China (too rich, given its lack of democracy) and India (not rich enough, given its “vibrant political institutions”). The chart indicated two ways in which India might converge to the global mean: fast growth or institutional decline.
Encouraged by the success of his surveys, Mr Subramanian has adopted the same approach (charts, arguments, catchy phrases) in an ambitious book, written with Devesh Kapur of Johns Hopkins University. It re-examines India’s growth record, social divisions and state apparatus over the past 75 years. “A Sixth of Humanity” is not short, spanning over 600 pages. But plenty of books about America require as many pages to cover a quarter as many people. The authors’ accomplishment is all the more remarkable given India’s forbidding complexity. The sixth of humanity within its compass is not much easier to summarise than any other sixth scattered across national borders elsewhere. India has 325 languages, according to one study, and no fewer than 24 scripts.
India’s growth trajectory, like its population, is a bit of a jumble. It has pursued what the authors call a “precocious” model of development, doing things in a peculiar order. Its democracy outpaced its development and its skilled service industries outran its labour-intensive manufacturing. It prioritised universities before schools, hospitals before clinics, contraception before sanitation. The state ventured widely (and wastefully) into business before deigning to roll out much infrastructure. It has also dispensed cash transfers to citizens’ bank accounts before providing public amenities, like clean air or good schools for all. The state machinery that holds India together is surprisingly small. The country has only half as many coppers per person as England and Wales. Its civil engineers were slow to bind the nation with roads, tunnels and bridges. London has over 50 ways to cross its defining river; Kolkata just five. The Indian state has also failed to properly title or tax the land **under its writ**. There was no full land survey in Bihar, one of India’s biggest states, from 1911 until the 2020s. By then few officers could read the nearly extinct script in which many old documents were written. Land disputes have declined in recent years, the book notes. Economic growth has given the state more money to spend on compensating owners. The public investment enabled by less **tortuous **land purchases has in turn helped underpin growth.
stem: What surprised Arvind Subramanian about the reception of his annual Economic Survey?

options.a: It was criticised for being excessively theoretical and detached from policy needs
options.b: It attracted a far wider readership than he had originally anticipated
options.c: It failed to generate debate among policymakers and economists
options.d: It was seen as repetitive despite being released every year
options.e: It was overshadowed by other official government publications

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 27) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in **bold** to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
The AI Summit, New Delhi emerged as a seminal congregation of policymakers, technocrats, banking magnates, and academic luminaries, all converging to deliberate upon the transformative potential of artificial intelligence in reshaping India’s economic and financial architecture. Convened at a time when algorithmic intelligence is no longer a speculative abstraction but a tangible driver of productivity, the summit underscored the imperative of fostering innovation while safeguarding ethical integrity.
In his inaugural address, the Finance Minister articulated a compelling vision of India as a global epicenter of responsible AI development. He accentuated that the banking sector, traditionally perceived as conservative, is now undergoing a paradigmatic **metamorphosis**. From predictive analytics in credit appraisal to AI-driven fraud detection systems, financial institutions are leveraging machine learning algorithms to **augment** efficiency and mitigate systemic risks. The discourse emphasized that AI is not intended to supplant human judgment but to complement it, thereby engendering a symbiotic relationship between technology and human acumen.
A salient theme of the summit was financial inclusion. Experts elucidated how AI-powered chatbots and vernacular language models can democratize access to banking services, especially in rural hinterlands. By analyzing alternative data streams, such as transactional behavior and micro-savings patterns, banks can extend credit to previously marginalized segments, thereby fostering inclusive growth. Nevertheless, speakers also cautioned against the inadvertent exacerbation of digital divides, urging regulators to institute robust data protection frameworks.
Cybersecurity emerged as another pivotal concern. With the proliferation of digital transactions, the susceptibility to cyber **malfeasance** has intensified. AI-enabled surveillance systems, capable of real-time anomaly detection, were showcased as instrumental in preempting financial crimes. However, participants warned that overreliance on opaque algorithms could engender opacity and erode public trust if not accompanied by transparency and accountability.
The summit culminated in the adoption of the “Delhi Declaration on Ethical AI,” a comprehensive charter advocating fairness, explainability, and sustainability in AI deployment. It exhorted banks and fintech enterprises to adhere to stringent compliance standards while nurturing innovation. The declaration also envisaged collaborative research initiatives between academia and industry to cultivate indigenous AI capabilities.
In essence, the AI Summit in New Delhi epitomized India’s resolute commitment to harnessing artificial intelligence as a catalyst for equitable economic advancement. By harmonizing technological ingenuity with prudent regulation, the nation aspires to consolidate its position as a vanguard in the global AI ecosystem.
stem: What was the primary objective of the AI Summit in New Delhi?

options.b: To deliberate on AI’s role in economic and financial transformation

In his inaugural address, the Finance Minister articulated a compelling vision of India as a global epicenter of responsible AI development. He accentuated that the banking sector, traditionally perceived as conservative, is now undergoing a paradigmatic **metamorphosis**. From predictive analytics in credit appraisal to AI-driven fraud detection systems, financial institutions are leveraging machine learning algorithms to **augment** efficiency and mitigate systemic risks. The discourse emphasized that AI is not intended to supplant human judgment but to complement it, thereby engendering a symbiotic relationship between technology and human acumen.
A salient theme of the summit was financial inclusion. Experts elucidated how AI-powered chatbots and vernacular language models can democratize access to banking services, especially in rural hinterlands. By analyzing alternative data streams, such as transactional behavior and micro-savings patterns, banks can extend credit to previously marginalized segments, thereby fostering inclusive growth. Nevertheless, speakers also cautioned against the inadvertent exacerbation of digital divides, urging regulators to institute robust data protection frameworks.
Cybersecurity emerged as another pivotal concern. With the proliferation of digital transactions, the susceptibility to cyber **malfeasance** has intensified. AI-enabled surveillance systems, capable of real-time anomaly detection, were showcased as instrumental in preempting financial crimes. However, participants warned that overreliance on opaque algorithms could engender opacity and erode public trust if not accompanied by transparency and accountability.
The summit culminated in the adoption of the “Delhi Declaration on Ethical AI,” a comprehensive charter advocating fairness, explainability, and sustainability in AI deployment. It exhorted banks and fintech enterprises to adhere to stringent compliance standards while nurturing innovation. The declaration also envisaged collaborative research initiatives between academia and industry to cultivate indigenous AI capabilities.
In essence, the AI Summit in New Delhi epitomized India’s resolute commitment to harnessing artificial intelligence as a catalyst for equitable economic advancement. By harmonizing technological ingenuity with prudent regulation, the nation aspires to consolidate its position as a vanguard in the global AI ecosystem.

set_title: IBPS CSA-XVI PRELIMS 2026 (MODEL TEST 25) - Reading comprehension
passage:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it. Certain words are given in **bold** to help you locate them while answering some of the questions.
Lignosat’s communications failed as it was launched from the International Space Station (iss) on December 9th 2024. But it was a breakthrough all the same. For much of it was made of magnolia, a wood its builders at Kyoto University had picked for its strength, ease of working and (as demonstrated by previous experiments on the iss) **resilience** to the **hostile** environment of space. It proved a good choice. Though LignoSat’s temperature oscillated from -100 to +100°C as it passed in and out of Earth’s shadow, and it was also bombarded by the radiation of the solar wind, its wooden panels held firm, according to tracking by America’s Space Force, until its fiery atmospheric re-entry 116 days later.
Huld, a Finnish firm, prefers birch plywood to magnolia for wisa Woodsat, a test vehicle it helped design that is due for launch this summer. Such plywood is routinely cooled to -163°C when used to insulate tanks carrying liquefied natural gas. Wood has several advantages over metal alloys as a satellite material. One is to reduce the amount of metal vaporising when satellites burn up on re-entry. In 2023 some 290 tonnes of space junk fell into the atmosphere. A study published that year found a tenth of the stratospheric sulphuric-acid particles it sampled contained such metal. How much that matters, if at all, is unclear. But some people fear a build-up of metals at altitude will trigger chemical reactions which might, for instance, destroy ozone, a form of oxygen that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. And build up they surely will. One forecast suggests that, by 2035, more than 2,800 tonnes of space junk a year will fall from orbit.
Swapping metal for wood, though, is not without hazard, observes Daniel Cziczo of Purdue University, who was one of the authors of the stratospheric-particle study. What might emerge from a reaction between the resulting soot and vaporised electronics remains unknown. Such fears are unlikely, however, to rule wood out as a space material, for it has another advantage. Regulators are tightening the “design for demise” rules, intended to stop chunks of falling spacecraft reaching the ground. Satellites weighing more than about 300kg usually need special guidance systems to comply with these rules by ensuring controlled re-entry into a deserted part of the ocean. Dr Sakraker’s team think incorporating wood, which would burn up in the atmosphere, might permit spacecraft weighing up to a tonne to duck that additional cost and re-enter uncontrolled.
stem: What was the main reason Kyoto University chose magnolia wood for LignoSat?

options.c: It showed strength and resilience in space conditions
options.d: It was easily available in America

Lignosat’s communications failed as it was launched from the International Space Station (iss) on December 9th 2024. But it was a breakthrough all the same. For much of it was made of magnolia, a wood its builders at Kyoto University had picked for its strength, ease of working and (as demonstrated by previous experiments on the iss) **resilience** to the **hostile** environment of space. It proved a good choice. Though LignoSat’s temperature oscillated from -100 to +100°C as it passed in and out of Earth’s shadow, and it was also bombarded by the radiation of the solar wind, its wooden panels held firm, according to tracking by America’s Space Force, until its fiery atmospheric re-entry 116 days later.
Huld, a Finnish firm, prefers birch plywood to magnolia for wisa Woodsat, a test vehicle it helped design that is due for launch this summer. Such plywood is routinely cooled to -163°C when used to insulate tanks carrying liquefied natural gas. Wood has several advantages over metal alloys as a satellite material. One is to reduce the amount of metal vaporising when satellites burn up on re-entry. In 2023 some 290 tonnes of space junk fell into the atmosphere. A study published that year found a tenth of the stratospheric sulphuric-acid particles it sampled contained such metal. How much that matters, if at all, is unclear. But some people fear a build-up of metals at altitude will trigger chemical reactions which might, for instance, destroy ozone, a form of oxygen that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. And build up they surely will. One forecast suggests that, by 2035, more than 2,800 tonnes of space junk a year will fall from orbit.
Swapping metal for wood, though, is not without hazard, observes Daniel Cziczo of Purdue University, who was one of the authors of the stratospheric-particle study. What might emerge from a reaction between the resulting soot and vaporised electronics remains unknown. Such fears are unlikely, however, to rule wood out as a space material, for it has another advantage. Regulators are tightening the “design for demise” rules, intended to stop chunks of falling spacecraft reaching the ground. Satellites weighing more than about 300kg usually need special guidance systems to comply with these rules by ensuring controlled re-entry into a deserted part of the ocean. Dr Sakraker’s team think incorporating wood, which would burn up in the atmosphere, might permit spacecraft weighing up to a tonne to duck that additional cost and re-enter uncontrolled.
